title: The Spirit urges Simeon to seize the blessing before the Magi; Simeon's thanksgiving and the evangelist's defense of calling Joseph father
english: appears, before the Magi arrive, so that we are not insulted. For the light that comes from me must anticipate the star's arrival in Bethlehem, so that it may be known that from me the star both receives guidance for its course and borrows its ray. But do not suffer loss, if the uncircumcised should harvest the firstfruits of the blessing.”

“And he blessed God and said: ‘Now you release your servant, Master, according to your word, in peace’” (Luke 2:28-29). He blessed God the Father together with the Son, and the Son together with the Spirit, because the Spirit was the one giving the oracle, while he held the Son in his arms—the Son who was pleased to appear in flesh and to become an infant for our sake. And the Father himself was also at work in mysteries so great and so mighty.

But for what did he offer thanksgiving? “Now,” he says, “you release your servant, Master,” because now I have no fear of death, but with joy I go to the dead, announcing life to them. “You release me according to your word, in peace”—that word which David the prophet, having borrowed from you, spoke: “In peace I will lie down and sleep” (Psalm 4:8).

“For my eyes have seen your salvation” (Luke 2:30), which many of the prophets desired to see. But now by actual experience you have presented to the human race the Most High, humbled for our sake to such a degree that he became an infant. For the potter could not otherwise save the ruined clay unless he himself was going to be mixed together with it. “My eyes have seen your salvation, which you prepared before the face of all the peoples” (Luke 2:30-31)—all of them, because being the creator of all, you necessarily set before all the mystery of salvation. “A light for revelation to the nations and glory for your people Israel” (Luke 2:32). First the nations are enlightened, and after this Israel is glorified. For this one was born for whom the first became last and the last became first, since those who were ahead lost the privileges of the front ranks through carelessness.

“And his father and his mother were marveling at what was being said about him” (Luke 2:33). Why do you call Joseph the father, O evangelist and writer of the divine genealogy? For you yourself showed that Gabriel spoke to the virgin when he explained how the conception would occur and in what manner the virgin would give birth: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke 1:35). “I have not forgotten my own words,” he says. “For even if I were forgetful, the Spirit would remind me. But the Incarnate One willed Joseph to be called father at that time, so that the one lying in wait against the mystery of our salvation might be deceived.” “They were marveling at what was being said about him,” because the old man was holding an infant, yet he was uttering hymns to God. “And Simeon blessed them” (Luke 2:34). For it was fitting that those who ministered the blessing to those under a curse should themselves be blessed.

title: Christ as fall and rising, and the sign contradicted
english: “And he said to Mary his mother, ‘Behold, this child lies for the fall and rising of many in Israel’” (Luke 2:34). For this is the one about whom Peter, taking up the prophecy of Isaiah, wrote to the churches: “Behold, I lay in Zion a cornerstone, chosen and precious, and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame” (1 Peter 2:6). Then he goes on, interpreting the prophecy and speaking in agreement with Simeon: “To you who believe, then, is the honor; but to those who disbelieve, the stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner, and a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense; they stumble because they disobey the word” (1 Peter 2:7-8). So he lay for the fall of the faithless and for the rising of the faithful. For those who thought they were standing according to the law cast themselves down by their unbelief; but these, though they were among the fallen because of the multitude of their sins, ran to the staff of faith and raised themselves up.

“Behold, this child lies for the fall and rising of many in Israel, and for a sign contradicted” (Luke 2:34). What is this? The cross. For that sign was contradicted because it was filled with both sufferings and wonders: he was naked and hid the sun; he was pierced with nails and shook the rocks; his side was opened by a spear and he opened the tombs of the dead. That is why the sign was contradicted. The faithless left aside the wonders and looked only at the sufferings, while the faithful saw the wonders together with the sufferings. So at that time the crowd of the Pharisees mocked him as a deceiver, but the centurion called him Son of God, and having said it, he worshiped.

What follows agrees with these things: “And a sword will pierce your own soul also, so that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed” (Luke 2:35). “A sword will pierce your soul”—that is, discernment will pass through at the time of the cross. For you will marvel when you see hanging on the cross the one born without destruction, the one conceived without a man, the one who passed through the womb without opening it and accomplished his own birth without suffering and without corruption.

And what will happen from this? “So that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed” (Luke 2:35). Perhaps the thoughts of others as well, but much more the thoughts of those who had been disciples of the Lord and had seen both the sufferings surrounding him and the wonders done by him, and had endured a storm from their thoughts on both sides. Cleopas suffered this, as Christ brought to light when he met him on the road to Emmaus. For when Cleopas was asked why they were downcast and troubled in heart, he spoke briefly about Christ—as much as the occasion allowed—not knowing to whom he was speaking, and then added: “But we had hoped that he was the one who was going to redeem Israel” (Luke 24:21). That is, things foreign to our hope have turned out concerning him.

title: Anna's widowhood and proclamation of redemption
english: Mary Magdalene’s thought lay open too, and it was weak. Her thought grew weak after Christ was crucified. She spoke to him without knowing him and said, “Sir, if you have carried him away, tell me where you have laid him, and I will take him away” (John 20:15).

Let the Gospel story run on and supply what remains. Luke says, “And Anna was a prophetess, the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher. She was far advanced in days, having lived with her husband seven years from her virginity, and she was a widow of about eighty-four years” (Luke 2:36) (Luke 2:37).

Anna’s wealth shines bright. Her store of good things gathers from every side. First, she was a prophetess. She bore a frail vessel, a woman’s body, and she cleansed it. She drew the Spirit of God to dwell in her. Second, she was aged, and though her body had grown old, her resolve had not grown old. Third, she was a widow, and no ordinary widow. She lived only seven years with her husband. She advanced many days and dragged the yoke of widowhood through so many years. She never gave her bed to a second bridegroom. So she drove her life into its eightieth year.

She had seen him whom the Spirit clearly proclaimed in the eighty-fourth psalm. So she longed to speak of him in words like those David the psalmist sang: “Lord, you favored your land; you turned back the captivity of Jacob. You forgave the iniquities of your people; you covered all their sins. You stilled all your anger; you turned away from your fierce wrath” (Psalms 85:1-3); “Truth has sprung from the earth, and righteousness has looked down from heaven” (Psalms 85:11). In these words lies the redemption of Jerusalem, which Luke next says this woman proclaimed and prophesied. For Luke says, “She did not leave the temple” (Luke 2:37). Many live in the temple, yet living there they insult it. They do not dwell as Anna dwelt, “serving night and day with fasts and prayers” (Luke 2:37). By fasting she cleansed her body. By prayer she gave wings to her soul. She dwelt as a temple within the temple.

Luke adds, “And coming up at that very hour” (Luke 2:38). The Spirit surely brought her, as it brought Simeon, to praise the infant. Luke says, “She was giving thanks in return to God” (Luke 2:38). She was not merely praising. She was answering God with praise, crying out words much like Simeon’s. Luke says, “And she spoke of him to all who were awaiting redemption in Jerusalem” (Luke 2:38). What was she saying? “Do not be led astray by his flesh. Do not stumble at the form of a servant. Do not let the infant trouble you.”

He fashions infants, yet he appears as an infant and a child. He is seen as a babe, yet he is the Father of ages. We could not have beheld the Redeemer otherwise. We could not have received him otherwise. For our sake he humbled himself. For our sake he came down. He spares our eyes. He hides his glory and puts forward his lowliness. To him be glory forever and ever. Amen.
